working: One-one: f(p) = f(q) gives (p-m)(q-n) = (q-m)(p-n), which reduces to (p-q)(m-n) = 0, so p = q since m != n. Onto: solving y = (x-m)/(x-n) gives x = (yn-m)/(y-1), undefined at y = 1, so 1 is never attained and the range is R minus {1}, a proper subset of the codomain. Hence one-one into.

subtopic: Set Operations, Identities, and Cartesian Products of Sets
working: (A - B) U (A - C) = (A n B') U (A n C') = A n (B' U C') = A n (B n C)' by De Morgan = A - (B n C). Checked on a concrete instance: A = {1,2,3}, B = {2,3}, C = {3} gives (A-B) U (A-C) = {1} U {1,2} = {1,2}, and A - (B n C) = A - {3} = {1,2}, while A n (B n C) = {3} and A n (B - C) = {2}.

working: B = B n (A U B) = B n (A U C) = (B n A) U (B n C) = (A n C) U (B n C) = (A U B) n C = (A U C) n C = C, using both hypotheses. So B = C. A = B and A = C need not hold (take A = {1}, B = C = {2}), and A n B need not be empty.

subtopic: Relations — Properties, Cartesian Product, and Counting
working: Reflexive: a divides a for every natural a. Transitive: a|b and b|c imply a|c. Not symmetric: 2|4 but 4 does not divide 2, which also rules out 'equivalence relation'. So reflexive and transitive only.

subtopic: Interrelating AP, GP and HP
working: Put x = a-b, y = b-c, z = c-a, so x + y + z = 0 identically. The hypothesis is 2y^2 = x^2 + z^2. From x + z = -y we get x^2 + z^2 = y^2 - 2xz, so 2y^2 = y^2 - 2xz, i.e. y^2 = -2xz, i.e. 2/y = -(y)/(xz) = (x+z)/(xz) = 1/x + 1/z. That is exactly the condition for 1/x, 1/y, 1/z to be in AP, and the step is reversible. Verified numerically with y = 1, x = -(1+sqrt3)/2, z = (sqrt3-1)/2: squares 1.866, 1, 0.134 are in AP and reciprocals -0.732, 1, 2.732 are in AP.

subtopic: Vieta's Relations and Root-Coefficient Identities
working: (x-a)(x-b) = c is x^2 - (a+b)x + (ab-c) = 0, so alpha + beta = a+b and alpha*beta = ab-c. Then (x-alpha)(x-beta) + c = x^2 - (a+b)x + (ab-c) + c = x^2 - (a+b)x + ab = (x-a)(x-b), whose roots are a and b.

subtopic: Vieta's Relations and Root-Coefficient Identities
working: Let the roots be r and r^2. Product r^3 = 3/3 = 1. r = 1 gives sum 2 = -p/3, i.e. p = -6, inadmissible since p > 0. The other cube roots of unity give roots omega and omega^2 with sum -1 = -p/3, so p = 3. Check: 3x^2 + 3x + 3 = 0 has roots omega, omega^2 and (omega)^2 = omega^2, so one root is indeed the square of the other.

subtopic: Computing Binomial Probabilities — Exact, At-Least, and Complementary Events
Probability via Counting
working: A sum of 6 with n dice needs compositions of 6 into n parts each between 1 and 6 (the upper bound never binds here). 4 dice: C(5,3) = 10 of 6^4 = 1296. 3 dice: C(5,2) = 10 of 216. 2 dice: 5 of 36. So the probabilities are 10/1296, 10/216, 5/36; multiplying all three by 1296 gives 10 : 60 : 180 = 1 : 6 : 18, in the stated order 4, 3, 2 dice. Counts verified by exhaustive enumeration.

subtopic: Event Algebra — Inclusion-Exclusion, Mutually Exclusive, Exhaustive
working: For mutually exclusive events P(A union B union C) = P(A)+P(B)+P(C) = 2/3 + 1/4 + 1/6 = 8/12+3/12+2/12 = 13/12, which exceeds 1. No probability can exceed 1, so this assignment is impossible and the statement is false.

working: One experiment is 3 tosses and 'success' is exactly 2 heads, with probability C(3,2)/2^3 = 3/8; so a single experiment fails with probability 5/8. Repeating the experiment 3 times independently, P(no success at all) = (5/8)^3 = 125/512.

subtopic: Probability via Counting
working: The product ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9 exactly when it is odd and not divisible by 5, which forces every factor's last digit into {1,3,7,9} (any factor ending in an even digit makes the product even; any ending in 5 makes it end in 5 or 0). Each factor's last digit is one of 10 equally likely digits, so the probability is (4/10)^4 = (2/5)^4 = 16/625. Verified by enumerating all 10^4 last-digit combinations: 256/10000 = 16/625.

subtopic: Event Algebra — Inclusion-Exclusion, Mutually Exclusive, Exhaustive

subtopic: Event Algebra — Inclusion-Exclusion, Mutually Exclusive, Exhaustive
working: A splits into (A intersect B) and (A intersect B'), so P(A intersect B') = P(A) - P(A intersect B) = 1/4 - 3/20 = 5/20 - 3/20 = 2/20 = 1/10.

subtopic: Event Algebra — Inclusion-Exclusion, Mutually Exclusive, Exhaustive
working: By De Morgan, A' intersect B' is the complement of A union B, so P(A' intersect B') = 1 - P(A union B) = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2.

The determinant becomes |1 1 1; 1 w w^2; 1 w^2 w| = (w^2 - w^4) - (w - w^2) + (w^2 - w) = 3(w^2 - w) = 3w(w-1). Numerically -3*sqrt(3)*i, which matches option B exactly; option D is its negative (+3*sqrt(3)*i) and option C is -1.5 - 2.598i.

working: Reading the denominator as iz+1 and putting z = x+iy, rationalising gives Im((2z+1)/(iz+1)) = (-x(2x+1) - 2y(y-1))/(x^2 + (y-1)^2). Setting that equal to -2 and clearing the denominator cancels the -2x^2 and -2y^2 terms on both sides and leaves x + 2y - 2 = 0, a straight line (strictly, the line minus the point (0,1) where the denominator vanishes -- that point does lie on the line).
notes: The stem prints the denominator's z carrying a DOT accent (pandoc 'overset dot over z'), which is not standard notation in a complex-locus problem -- a dot over z is a time derivative, meaningless here. I read it as plain z, the standard anthologised form of this problem, which yields the straight line x + 2y - 2 = 0. If instead the dot is a mangled CONJUGATE bar, i.e. Im((2z+1)/(i*conj(z)+1)) = -2, the same rationalisation gives -x + 4y^2 + 6y + 2 = 0, i.e. x = 4y^2 + 6y + 2, a PARABOLA -- option C. Both readings land on a printed option, so the option list does not disambiguate; the accent is the only evidence and it is ambiguous. subtopic: Determinant Properties, Operations, and Sums
working: A determinant equals that of its transpose, so A = |a b c; d e f; l m n|. B = |l m n; a b c; d e f| is that same matrix with its rows cyclically shifted (third row brought to the top), a 3-cycle and therefore an even permutation, so the determinant is unchanged: B = A and A - B = 0. Verified symbolically (A - B expands to 0, while A + B is twice a non-zero general expression, so option A fails).
